title: Wuthering Heights looks different when you listen to the woman who escaped
subtitle: Emily Brontë gave Heathcliff’s wife a voice, an account of abuse and a way out. The debate around Emerald Fennell’s adaptation raises a question larger than fidelity to a classic: whose suffering becomes expendable when a story is sold as romance?

body:
Original reporting date: 17 September 2026

When Isabella Linton writes home after marrying Heathcliff, she is no longer describing the man she imagined. She is trying to explain the man she fears. In Chapter 13 of Wuthering Heights, her letter to the housekeeper Nelly Dean asks: “Is Mr. Heathcliff a man?” What follows is an account of isolation, hostility and a marriage she does not know how to endure.

That letter unsettles any reading of Emily Brontë’s novel that allows Heathcliff’s devotion to Catherine Earnshaw to explain away what he does to other women. Isabella lives inside the consequences of his celebrated passion. Her testimony deserves the same attention as his grief.

https://www.gutenberg.org/files/768/768-h/768-h.htm

Emerald Fennell’s 2026 adaptation, starring Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi, has made that tension newly visible. Its international theatrical rollout began during Valentine’s week. In a February interview with Reuters, Fennell emphasised the central couple’s imperfections and the place of forgiveness in love. That is a defensible artistic interest. But forgiveness becomes a more difficult proposition when the person doing the forgiving is not the person who has been harmed.

https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/margot-robbie-delves-into-rollercoaster-romance-wuthering-heights-2026-02-06/

![The 1847 title page of the first edition of Wuthering Heights.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/64/Houghton_Lowell_1238.5_%28A%29_-_Wuthering_Heights%2C_1847.jpg)

The first-edition title page of Wuthering Heights, published under Emily Brontë’s pseudonym Ellis Bell, 1847. Lowell 1238.5 (A), Houghton Library, Harvard University; public domain. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Houghton_Lowell_1238.5_(A)_-_Wuthering_Heights,_1847.jpg

## Isabella contradicts the romantic hero

Brontë does not make Isabella an exemplary judge of character. She falls in love with a version of Heathcliff that he does not fulfil. Crucially, however, the novel allows her to revise her understanding.

In Chapter 14, Heathcliff mocks her for imagining him a “hero of romance”. He describes her suffering with contempt, then claims she could leave if she wished. Isabella immediately contradicts him: she has tried to go and is afraid to try again. The sequence matters. His explanation of her behaviour is not the novel’s final word. The woman he is describing is present to challenge it.

https://www.gutenberg.org/files/768/768-h/768-h.htm

This is where the book becomes especially useful to a discussion of romanticised violence. An abusive character can claim that a woman secretly enjoys her treatment. A story can expose that claim by allowing her to answer. If an adaptation instead supplies images that appear to confirm him, the meaning changes—even when some of the dialogue remains intact.

Fennell’s treatment of Isabella makes precisely this question unavoidable. Entertainment Weekly’s February interview describes a scene in which she wears a dog collar, is chained by the fireplace and winks at Nelly. Fennell said the wink was deliberately retained for its disturbing contrast with the image; she also defended the scene’s close use of Brontë’s dialogue. Elordi described the marriage as a kind of hell. These accounts complicate any claim that the filmmakers simply intended a happy or healthy relationship.

https://ew.com/jacob-elordi-and-alison-oliver-on-that-wuthering-heights-dog-collar-scene-11899936

Nevertheless, a wink changes whose account the audience is invited to trust. It can encourage viewers to read apparent humiliation as private enjoyment. That is an interpretation of the scene’s construction, not evidence that every viewer understands it that way.

Consensual submission and domestic abuse are different things. There is nothing inherently progressive or regressive about a fictional woman enjoying a submissive sexual role. The sharper question is what happens when that role replaces a particular woman’s account of coercion. Giving a character sexual desire does not, by itself, preserve her freedom to refuse, leave or describe harm.

## The part of her story that matters most

Isabella eventually escapes. In Chapter 17, she recounts an assault and her flight across the moor, then leaves the neighbourhood. She subsequently gives birth to her son away from Heathcliff. Her story includes fear, anger and the effort to build a separate life. She does not redeem him through sufficient patience.

https://www.gutenberg.org/files/768/768-h/768-h.htm

The distinction matters because “agency” can become an oddly narrow compliment in discussions of female characters. A woman may be called empowered because she desires, seduces or participates, while her ability to withdraw receives less attention. Isabella’s departure offers another measure: whether she can stop organising her life around the man at the centre of the story.

![Portrait detail of Emily Brontë painted by her brother Patrick Branwell Brontë.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fc/Emily_Bront%C3%AB_by_Patrick_Branwell_Bront%C3%AB_restored.jpg)

Emily Brontë, from a portrait of the Brontë sisters by Patrick Branwell Brontë, created before his death in 1848. National Portrait Gallery collection; restored public-domain image by Dcoetzee. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Emily_Bront%C3%AB_by_Patrick_Branwell_Bront%C3%AB_restored.jpg
https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/

There is a related cost to concentrating on the novel’s first generation. Fennell has defended her film as a personal interpretation rather than a comprehensive adaptation; People reported that it covers only the first half of the story.

https://people.com/emerald-fennell-defends-controversial-changes-wuthering-heights-11907767

Brontë continues into the lives of the children who inherit the older generation’s hostility. Later, the younger Catherine and Hareton begin to move towards companionship through apology, reading and a gradual change in how they treat one another. Their relationship is imperfect, but its movement offers a counterpoint to possession and revenge: intimacy requires altered behaviour.

https://www.gutenberg.org/files/768/768-h/768-h.htm

An adaptation is entitled to choose a different ending or emphasis. Those choices also determine what the audience is left with: the grandeur of consuming passion, or the possibility of living beyond it.

None of this requires women to defend enjoying difficult fiction. Attraction to a dangerous fictional character is not proof of wanting an unsafe relationship, and literary analysis cannot establish that watching a film causes someone to accept abuse. The responsibility of criticism is to examine what a work asks us to notice, excuse or forget.

Wuthering Heights can sustain fascination with Heathcliff and scrutiny of his cruelty at once. What it cannot sustain without losing something essential is a reading in which his capacity to love one woman makes another woman’s suffering incidental. Isabella has already told us what that love story looks like from inside his house. Listening to her changes the book.
